Chapter Eight: Integrating Unconscious Wisdom Into Relationships
You know, if there’s ever a place where our unconscious mind shows up loud and clear, it’s in our relationships. Think about it—those old patterns, the fears we never quite voice, the needs we sometimes don’t even know we have... All of that can bubble up when we’re close to someone, whether it’s a partner, a friend, or even a coworker.
Let’s imagine a couple who’s been married for years. Week after week, they find themselves stuck in the same old argument. Maybe it sounds like it’s about chores, or money—but underneath the surface, it’s really about something much deeper. One of them just wants to feel seen. The other is scared they’re not enough.
Through gentle, honest conversations, they start to notice the stories they each bring from their past—a childhood of feeling invisible for one, a lifelong worry of falling short for the other. And when they share those deeper truths, something starts to shift. Suddenly, it’s not about winning or losing the fight. They’re on the same team, working to understand the roots of their hurt.
Here’s something to pay attention to: most of the time, our conflicts aren’t really about the thing we’re arguing about. They’re about the hidden beliefs and emotions that are shaping our reactions. So next time you find yourself locked in a disagreement, try pausing and asking, what’s really going on here? That tiny moment of curiosity can move you past blame and defensiveness, straight into understanding.
And let’s talk a bit about empathy. We’ve touched on it before, but here, it gets even deeper. It’s not just about tuning in to what someone else is feeling—it’s about noticing the unconscious drivers behind their actions. Imagine a parent, worn out by a child’s tantrum, who suddenly realizes there’s fear or confusion beneath the yelling. Or a friend, hurt by silence, recognizing that an old wound might be fueling the distance.
The book offers some really practical tools you can use, like reflective listening—where you repeat back not just the words you hear, but the feelings underneath. Or try “owning” your emotions: instead of saying, you never care about my time, try, I feel scared when you’re late. These simple shifts open the door for honesty, and, over time, for healing.
There’s a story that sticks with me—a manager, famous for being tough but fair, is caught off guard when a team member breaks down in tears during a review. Instead of brushing it off, the manager pauses, remembering what it felt like to be new and afraid of not measuring up. She offers a bit of reassurance. And just like that, the conversation changes. The team member leaves feeling truly seen, and the manager feels this quiet pride in her own growth.
So here’s the heart of it: relationships will never be perfect. But they’re amazing places to learn and grow. When we bring our unconscious wisdom into the open, we can build connections that are more honest, more compassionate, and so much stronger than before.
